Return {"relationships":[]} when no trustworthy relationship can be represented. Return no Markdown fences, prose, comments, or adjacent documents. Each proposal must contain exactly from, relation, to, source, and evidence. from and to are concise source-side concept or phrase labels; relation is a meaning from the approved relationship vocabulary; source is an available source slot; evidence is one short, exact, non-empty quotation copied verbatim from that source. Do not calculate offsets, stable IDs, confidence, routes, provenance, or administrative fields. Do not invent relationship labels. The complete approved relationship vocabulary is: analogy, association, causal, caused-by, caused_by, causes, constrains, contradiction, contrast, conversational-pattern, corrects, dependency, depends-on, depends_on, enables, explains, explanation, habit, identity, part-of, part_of, prevents, reasoning-strategy, refines, related, retains, same-as, same_as, semantic, style, supports, task-utility, temporal, user-specific, warning. Return at most six proposals. Fewer is normal and preferable to guessing. Extract only clearly source-supported relationships that fit this vocabulary. Ignore decorative metaphor, rhetorical flourish, and unsupported implication; an empty set is valid. Do not literalize figurative language. Keep each record concise. Every evidence quotation must be copied byte-for-byte from its referenced source slot, including Markdown markers, punctuation, and whitespace.

eligible.content: It really was—like the shed decided to remind me it’s not all tangled wires and expired batteries. That jar’s been sitting there since August, quietly doing its own thing, and still ended up exactly what I needed this morning with my tea. Makes you wonder what else is hiding in plain sight, just waiting for the right moment to be useful. Or delicious. Or both.

Yeah, but honestly? I almost tossed that jar thinking it was ruined. Took me a minute to remember honey doesn’t really go bad—it just gets firm and opinionated. Kind of like my aunt, actually. Point is, if I’d cleared the shelf last fall like I said I would, I’d have thrown out the good with the clutter. Makes me wonder how many other "ruined" things are just waiting for someone to warm them up a little and give them another chance. Anyway—back to the lantern. Still doesn’t work. But at least I’ve got honey.

Sure, if you want to call it magic—though my dad would just say it’s called “not throwing stuff out.” But honestly, it’s not just the honey. Found the lantern’s wiring’s chewed through, probably mice. So now I’m trying to decide if it’s cheaper to patch it with spare wire from the old speaker or just admit I’ve got to buy new. Either way, I can’t let one broken thing stop the whole fix. That’s how the shed wins.
"It seems like a classic case of needing a little patience and a practical problem-solving mindset. You've got a choice to make—whether to perform a DIY patch or invest in a complete replacement."
